c: Eight labels describe what kind of claim each sentence is. Confidence and source access are tracked separately.
Every important sentence carries a label. Tap it to see the sources. A page can mix labels — a patient observation next to a research finding next to a hypothesis — and each keeps its own status.
: What a national guideline, regulator or product licence says. Guidance shapes practice; it does not guarantee a particular prescription.
: A finding from published research. Check the study design: a trial, a registry comparison and a case report carry very different weight.
: What an NHS body or service has said or decided, in its own records. It shows their position, not that the position is correct.
: What a patient observed or reported. Recorded by a clinician or not, it remains a report until measured or independently corroborated.
: A proposed explanation that has not been tested. Included because it generates useful questions — never as a basis for changing treatment alone.
: Two or more accounts of the same event disagree. Both are shown; neither is treated as settled until records resolve it.
: A source that should exist and has not been obtained or checked. Absence from reviewed records does not mean the event did not happen.
: A formal finding by a body with authority to make it — a coroner, ombudsman, regulator or court.
What kind of claim is it?
— confidence: strong, moderate, limited or pending.
— access: full text, abstract, supplied document, or pointer only. A strong study read only in abstract is still marked as abstract.
